text: Abortions. Am I pro-choice or am I pro-life? This is a question I get asked a lot. And the simple answer is, I'm a little bit of both. Let me explain. From what I understand, when people debate abortion, there are usually two major questions. When does the embryo or fetus become alive that we should morally protect? And the second is, even after that point, does a woman's bodily autonomy still give her the right to terminate the pregnancy? And let me make one thing clear. I'm not claiming to have the ultimate truth. This is simply my opinion based on the information I have as of now. But first things first. When does the embryo or fetus become alive that we should morally protect? Because I think almost everyone on both sides agrees on one very basic principle. Taking an innocent human life is wrong. The disagreement is over when exactly the embryo or fetus becomes a human being in the moral sense. And obviously, when I say life, I don't simply mean biologically alive. Because individual cells are biologically alive. What I mean is, at what point has the embryo or fetus developed enough that we should consider it a human person whose life deserves moral protection? I believe people who talk about abortions have a term for this. Moral status. And there is no universal agreement on when full moral status begins. Some people say conception. Some say birth. But the broad legal and social compromise in many western countries is gradualist. Early pregnancy is treated differently from late pregnancy, with a major practical line around 12 to 14 weeks, and a much stronger moral and legal concern around viability, roughly 24 weeks. Personally, I don't think it starts at conception. But I also don't believe that a fetus six months into pregnancy has essentially the same moral status as a fertilized egg from yesterday. So for me, somewhere in between, the situation changes. When and where exactly? I don't know. Let's take cardiac development just as an example. Early cardiac activity can be detected at around six weeks. But at that point, we're obviously not talking about a fully developed heart. Development continues after that. So where exactly do we draw the line? Six weeks? Ten weeks? Somewhere in between? For the sake of argument, let's say eight weeks. And I am not saying that science proves that moral status magically begins at exactly eight weeks. I'm just choosing a hypothetical point to explain how I think about abortion. Before that point, I am generally pro-choice. The woman should be able to decide whether she wants to continue the pregnancy. After that point, I become much more restrictive. Not because pregnancy suddenly stops affecting the woman's body, but because now I think there are two morally serious interests in conflict. And that brings us to the second major question, bodily autonomy. Because some people would argue that even if the fetus has moral status, it is still inside the woman's body. And therefore, she should have the right to terminate the pregnancy. And this is where I move much closer to the pro-life side. If we've already concluded that the fetus has developed enough that we consider it another human being with a right to life, then I don't think bodily autonomy by itself is sufficient justification to take its life. At that point, it's no longer only about one person's body. There are now two sets of rights involved. That doesn't mean abortion could never be justified after that point. If continuing the pregnancy creates a serious threat to the mother's life or health, for example, then obviously you are dealing with a much more difficult conflict. But simply saying, my body, my choice, would no longer be enough for me once I believe another human life with moral status is involved. So am I pro-choice or pro-life? Before moral status, generally pro-choice. After moral status, generally pro-life, with exceptions for serious circumstances. The part I find difficult isn't deciding what I believe on either side of the line. It is deciding where exactly that line should be.
